name: Radiomics
title: Radiomics
answer: Radiomics is the extraction of large numbers of quantitative features from medical images, most often CT, MRI and PET scans, and the use of those features to build models that describe a tumour or tissue beyond what the eye can see. It sits inside diagnostic imaging and radiology, where it overlaps with computer vision, oncology and pathology. A radiomics study typically begins with a segmented region of interest, such as a tumour outline, and ends with a statistical or machine learning model that predicts something like response to treatment or survival. The field is distinct from ordinary visual reading because it treats the image as a source of measurable data rather than only a picture.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Radiomics is the extraction of large numbers of quantitative features from medical images, most often CT, MRI and PET scans, and the use of those features to build models that describe a tumour or tissue beyond what the eye can see. It sits inside diagnostic imaging and radiology, where it overlaps with computer vision, oncology and pathology. A radiomics study typically begins with a segmented region of interest, such as a tumour outline, and ends with a statistical or machine learning model that predicts something like response to treatment or survival. The field is distinct from ordinary visual reading because it treats the image as a source of measurable data rather than only a picture.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on standard clinical imaging hardware plus a software pipeline that sits alongside the scanner. Images are pulled from PACS, converted to a consistent format, and processed on workstations or on shared compute, sometimes with GPU acceleration for the feature extraction and modelling steps. Open tools such as PyRadiomics are widely used for feature calculation, and segmentation is often done with commercial contouring software or with deep learning models that automate the outlining. Because the raw material is patient imaging, storage, transfer and processing all sit inside the hospital or vendor environment rather than on ordinary consumer infrastructure.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical study moves through several stages: image acquisition, segmentation of the region of interest, feature extraction, feature selection, and model building with validation. Features describe shape, intensity and texture, and the same tumour can yield hundreds or thousands of them, which makes selection and stability testing essential. Reproducibility is a known weak point, because small differences in scanner settings, slice thickness, reconstruction kernel or the exact contour can shift feature values. Good practice therefore includes a documented pipeline, a held out test set, and reporting that follows agreed checklists so another group can repeat the work.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Radiomics uses identifiable medical images, so it falls under the same privacy and research rules as other clinical data, including consent, de-identification and institutional review.Provenance matters because a model trained on one scanner or one hospital may not transfer to another, and the version of the segmentation, the feature library and the code all affect the result. Where a radiomics model is offered as a clinical product rather than a research finding, it enters the medical device framework, and the site's tracking of 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies shows that clinical AI claims can end up in court.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward standardisation and toward combining hand crafted radiomic features with deep learning, rather than treating them as rivals. Larger multi centre datasets and shared reporting standards are slowly making results more comparable, and automated segmentation is removing one of the biggest sources of variability. The open question is whether radiomics adds enough beyond a good deep learning model and clinical variables to justify the extra pipeline, and that is being tested prospectively rather than only in retrospective studies. As with any diagnostic tool, the value will be settled by whether it changes decisions and outcomes in real clinical use.
